content: Hormonal contraceptives may not provide reliable birth control when used concurrently with certain medications. Co-administration can increase the likelihood of menstrual-related side effects, such as amenorrhea, dysmenorrhea, or menorrhagia. For example: 1. Ritonavir can increase the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by altering its metabolism through the CYP3A4 enzyme. This may reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives. Alternative or additional non-hormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. 2. A sugammadex bolus dose is equivalent to missing doses of hormonal contraceptives. Patients using oral, transdermal, or implantable hormonal contraceptives on the same day as sugammadex should use additional non-hormonal contraception (e.g., condoms and spermicides) for the next 7 days. 3. St. John’s Wort decreases the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially reducing contraceptive efficacy. Non-hormonal contraceptive methods are recommended. 4. Tipranavir increases the levels or effects of norethindrone and ethinyl estradiol by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Significant changes in estrogen plasma levels may occur, reducing contraceptive efficacy. Non-hormonal contraception is advised. 5. Topiramate decreases the levels or effects of norethindrone and ethinyl estradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptives are not reliable in this case, and non-hormonal methods should be used. 6. Tucatinib increases norethindrone levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Concomitant use with CYP3A substrates should be avoided due to the risk of serious toxicities. If unavoidable, reduce the dose of the CYP3A substrate. 7. Antibiotics such as amoxicillin, ampicillin, cefaclor, cefadroxil, cefazolin, cefdinir, cefepime, cefixime, and others may decrease the levels or effects of ethinyl estradiol by altering intestinal flora. While the risk of contraceptive failure is low, caution and monitoring are advised. 8. Cenobamate decreases the levels or effects of norethindrone and ethinyl estradiol by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Women should use additional or alternative non-hormonal contraception during cenobamate treatment. 9. Clobazam decreases the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Additional non-hormonal contraception is recommended. 10. Elagolix decreases norethindrone and ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Monitor CYP3A substrates and consider dose adjustments. 11. Darunavir decreases ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism, potentially reducing contraceptive efficacy. Non-hormonal contraception is recommended. 12. Grapefruit increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. 13. Exenatide may reduce the absorption of oral contraceptives due to its effect on slowing gastric emptying. Patients should take oral contraceptives at least 1 hour before exenatide administration. 14. Fluconazole increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 15. Fostemsavir increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting BCRP transporters. Avoid co-administration or adjust the dose of BCRP substrates. 16. Insulin (various types) may have reduced hypoglycemic effects when used with ethinyl estradiol or norethindrone due to impaired glucose tolerance caused by estrogens or progestins. Monitor glycemic control in diabetic patients. 17. Istradefylline increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and monitoring are advised. In summary, many medications can alter the metabolism or effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives, either by increasing or decreasing their levels through interactions with hepatic or intestinal enzymes (e.g., CYP3A4).
